title: The Mastermaid

text:
Once on a time there was a king who had several sons—I don’t know how
many there were—but the youngest had no rest at home, for nothing else
would please him but to go out into the world and try his luck, and
after a long time the king was forced to give him leave to go. Now,
after he had travelled some days, he came one night to a Giant’s house,
and there he got a place in the Giant’s service. In the morning the
Giant went off to herd his goats, and as he left the yard, he told the
Prince to clean out the stable; “and after you have done that, you
needn’t do anything else to-day; for you must know it is an easy master
you have come to. But what is set you to do you must do well, and you
mustn’t think of going into any of the rooms which are beyond that in
which you slept, for if you do, I’ll take your life.”

“Sure enough, it is an easy master I have got”, said the Prince to
himself, as he walked up and down the room, and carolled and sang, for
he thought there was plenty of time to clean out the stable.

“But still it would be good fun just to peep into his other rooms, for
there must be something in them which he is afraid lest I should see,
since he won’t give me leave to go in.”

So he went into the first room, and there was a pot boiling on a hook
by the wall, but the Prince saw no fire underneath it. I wonder what is
inside it, he thought; and then he dipped a lock of his hair into it,
and the hair seemed as if it were all turned to copper.

“What a dainty broth,” he said; “if one tasted it, he’d look grand
inside his gullet”; and with that he went into the next room. There,
too, was a pot hanging by a hook, which bubbled and boiled; but there
was no fire under that either.

“I may as well try this too”, said the Prince, as he put another lock
into the pot, and it came out all silvered.

“They haven’t such rich broth in my father’s house”, said the Prince;
“but it all depends on how it tastes”, and with that he went on into
the third room. There, too, hung a pot, and boiled just as he had seen
in the two other rooms, and the Prince had a mind to try this too, so
he dipped a lock of hair into it, and it came out gilded, so that the
light gleamed from it.

“‘Worse and worse’, said the old wife; but I say better and better”,
said the Prince; “but if he boils gold here, I wonder what he boils in
yonder.”

He thought he might as well see; so he went through the door into the
fourth room. Well, there was no pot in there, but there was a Princess,
seated on a bench, so lovely, that the Prince had never seen anything
like her in his born days.

“Oh! in Heaven’s name”, she said, “what do you want here?”

“I got a place here yesterday”, said the Prince.

“A place, indeed! Heaven help you out of it.”

“Well, after all, I think I’ve got an easy master; he hasn’t set me
much to do to-day, for after I have cleaned out the stable, my day’s
work is over.”

“Yes, but how will you do it”, she said; “for if you set to work to
clean it like other folk, ten pitchforks full will come in for every
one you toss out. But I will teach you how to set to work; you must
turn the fork upside down, and toss with the handle, and then all the
dung will fly out of itself.”

“Yes, he would be sure to do that”, said the Prince; and so he sat
there the whole day, for he and the Princess were soon great friends,
and had made up their minds to have one another, and so the first day
of his service with the Giant was not long, you may fancy. But when the
evening drew on, she said “twould be as well if he got the stable
cleaned out before the Giant came home; and when he went to the stable,
he thought he would just see if what she had said were true, and so he
began to work like the grooms in his father’s stable; but he soon had
enough of that, for he hadn’t worked a minute before the stable was so
full of dung that he hadn’t room to stand. Then he did as the Princess
bade him, and turned up the fork and worked with the handle, and lo! in
a trice the stable was as clean as if it had been scoured. And when he
had done his work, he went back into the room where the Giant had given
him leave to be, and began to walk up and down, and to carol and sing.
So after a bit, home came the Giant with his goats.

“Have you cleaned the stable?” asked the Giant.

“Yes, now it’s all right and tight, master”, answered the Prince.

“I’ll soon see if it is”, growled the Giant, and strode off to the
stable, where he found it just as the Prince had said.

“You’ve been talking to my Mastermaid, I can see”, said the Giant; “for
you’ve not sucked this knowledge out of your own breast.”

“Mastermaid!” said the Prince, who looked as stupid as an owl, “what
sort of thing is that, master? I’d be very glad to see it.”

“Well, well!” said the Giant; “you’ll see her soon enough”.

Next day the Giant set off with his goats again, and before he went he
told the Prince to fetch home his horse, which was out at grass on the
hill-side, and when he had done that he might rest all the day.

“For you must know, it is an easy master you have come to”, said the
Giant; “but if you go into any of the rooms I spoke of yesterday, I’ll
wring your head off.”

So off he went with his flock of goats.

“An easy master you are indeed”, said the Prince; “but for all that,
I’ll just go in and have a chat with your Mastermaid; may be she’ll be
as soon mine as yours.” So he went in to her, and she asked him what he
had to do that day.

“Oh! nothing to be afraid of”, said he; “I’ve only to go up to the
hill-side to fetch his horse.”

“Very well, and how will you set about it?”

“Well, for that matter, there’s no great art in riding a horse home. I
fancy I’ve ridden fresher horses before now”, said the Prince.

“Ah, but this isn’t so easy a task as you think; but I’ll teach you how
to do it. When you get near it, fire and flame will come out of its
nostrils, as out of a tar barrel; but look out, and take the bit which
hangs behind the door yonder, and throw it right into his jaws, and he
will grow so tame that you may do what you like with him.”

Yes! the Prince would mind and do that; and so he sat in there the
whole day, talking and chattering with the Mastermaid about one thing
and another, but they always came back to how happy they would be if
they could only have one another, and get well away from the Giant;
and, to tell the truth, the Prince would have clean forgotten both the
horse and the hill-side, if the Mastermaid hadn’t put him in mind of
them when evening drew on, telling him he had better set out to fetch
the horse before the Giant came home. So he set off, and took the bit
which hung in the corner, ran up the hill, and it wasn’t long before he
met the horse, with fire and flame streaming out of its nostrils. But
he watched his time, and, as the horse came open-jawed up to him, he
threw the bit into its mouth, and it stood as quiet as a lamb. After
that, it was no great matter to ride it home and put it up, you may
fancy; and then the Prince went into his room again, and began to carol
and sing.

So the Giant came home again at even with his goats; and the first
words he said were:

“Have you brought my horse down from the hill?”

“Yes, master, that I have”, said the Prince; “and a better horse I
never bestrode; but for all that I rode him straight home, and put him
up safe and sound.”

“I’ll soon see to that”, said the Giant, and ran out to the stable, and
there stood the horse just as the Prince had said.

“You’ve talked to my Mastermaid, I’ll be bound, for you haven’t sucked
this out of your own breast”, said the Giant again.

“Yesterday master talked of this Mastermaid, and to-day it’s the same
story”, said the Prince, who pretended to be silly and stupid. “Bless
you, master! why don’t you show me the thing at once? I should so like
to see it only once in my life.”

“Oh, if that’s all”, said the Giant, “you’ll see her soon enough.”

The third day, at dawn, the Giant went off to the wood again with his
goats; but before he went he said to the Prince:

“To-day you must go to Hell and fetch my fire-tax. When you have done
that you can rest yourself all day, for you must know it is an easy
master you have come to”; and with that off he went.

“Easy master, indeed!” said the Prince. “You may be easy, but you set
me hard tasks all the same. But I may as well see if I can find your
Mastermaid, as you call her. I daresay she’ll tell me what to do”; and
so in he went to her again.

So when the Mastermaid asked what the Giant had set him to do that day,
he told her how he was to go to Hell and fetch the fire-tax.

“And how will you set about it?” asked the Mastermaid.

“Oh, that you must tell me”, said the Prince. “I have never been to
Hell in my life; and even if I knew the way, I don’t know how much I am
to ask for.”

“Well, I’ll soon tell you”, said the Mastermaid; “you must go to the
steep rock away yonder, under the hill-side, and take the club that
lies there, and knock on the face of the rock. Then there will come out
one all glistening with fire; to him you must tell your errand; and
when he asks you how much you will have, mind you say, ‘As much as I
can carry.’”

Yes; he would be sure to say that; so he sat in there with the
Mastermaid all that day too; and though evening drew on, he would have
sat there till now, had not the Mastermaid put him in mind that it was
high time to be off to Hell to fetch the Giant’s fire-tax before he
came home. So he went on his way, and did just as the Mastermaid had
told him; and when he reached the rock, he took up the club and gave a
great thump. Then the rock opened, and out came one whose face
glistened, and out of whose eyes and nostrils flew sparks of fire.

“What is your will?” said he.

“Oh! I’m only come from the Giant to fetch his fire-tax”, said the
Prince.

“How much will you have then?” said the other.

“I never wish for more than I am able to carry”, said the Prince.

“Lucky for you that you did not ask for a whole horse-load”, said he
who came out of the rock; “but come now into the rock with me, and you
shall have it.”

So the Prince went in with him, and you may fancy what heaps and heaps
of gold and silver he saw lying in there, just like stones in a gravel
pit; and he got a load just as big as he was able to carry, and set off
home with it. Now, when the Giant came home with his goats at even, the
Prince went into his room, and began to carol and sing as he had done
the evenings before.

“Have you been to Hell after my fire-tax?” roared the Giant.

“Oh yes; that I have, master”, answered the Prince.

“Where have you put it?” said the Giant.

“There stands the sack on the bench yonder”, said the Prince.

“I’ll soon see to that”, said the Giant, who strode off to the bench,
and there he saw the sack so full that the gold and silver dropped out
on the floor as soon as ever he untied the string.

“You’ve been talking to my Mastermaid, that I can see”, said the Giant;
“but if you have, I’ll wring your head off.”

“Mastermaid!” said the Prince; “yesterday master talked of this
Mastermaid, and to-day he talks of her again, and the day before
yesterday it was the same story. I only wish I could see what sort of
thing she is! that I do.”

“Well, well, wait till to-morrow”, said the Giant, “and then I’ll take
you in to her myself.”

“Thank you kindly, master”, said the Prince; “but it’s only a joke of
master’s, I’ll be bound.”

So next day the Giant took him in to the Mastermaid, and said to her:

“Now, you must cut his throat, and boil him in the great big pot you
wot of; and when the broth is ready, just give me a call.”

After that, he laid him down on the bench to sleep, and began to snore
so, that it sounded like thunder on the hills.

So the Mastermaid took a knife and cut the Prince in his little finger,
and let three drops of blood fall on a three-legged stool; and after
that she took all the old rags, and soles of shoes, and all the rubbish
she could lay hands on, and put them into the pot; and then she filled
a chest full of ground gold, and took a lump of salt, and a flask of
water that hung behind the door, and she took, besides, a golden apple,
and two golden chickens, and off she set with the Prince from the
Giant’s house as fast as they could; and when they had gone a little
way, they came to the sea, and after that they sailed over the sea; but
where they got the ship from, I have never heard tell.

So when the Giant had slumbered a good bit, he began to stretch himself
as he lay on the bench and called out, “Will it be soon done?”

“Only just begun”, answered the first drop of blood on the stool.

So the Giant lay down to sleep again, and slumbered a long, long time.
At last he began to toss about a little, and cried out:

“Do you hear what I say; will it be soon done?” but he did not look up
this time, any more than the first, for he was still half asleep.

“Half done”, said the second drop of blood.

Then the Giant thought again it was the Mastermaid, so he turned over
on his other side, and fell asleep again; and when he had gone on
sleeping for many hours, he began to stir and stretch his old bones,
and to call out,—

“Isn’t it done yet?”

“Done to a turn”, said the third drop of blood.

Then the Giant rose up and began to rub his eyes, but he couldn’t see
who it was that was talking to him, so he searched and called for the
Mastermaid, but no one answered.

“Ah, well! I dare say she’s just run out of doors for a bit”, he
thought, and took up a spoon and went up to the pot to taste the broth;
but he found nothing but shoe-soles, and rags, and such stuff; and it
was all boiled up together, so that he couldn’t tell which was thick
and which was thin. As soon as he saw this, he could tell how things
had gone, and he got so angry he scarce knew which leg to stand upon.
Away he went after the Prince and the Mastermaid, till the wind
whistled behind him; but before long, he came to the water and couldn’t
cross it.

“Never mind”, he said; “I know a cure for this. I’ve only got to call
on my stream-sucker.”

So he called on his stream-sucker, and he came and stooped down, and
took one, two, three gulps; and then the water fell so much in the sea,
that the Giant could see the Mastermaid and the Prince sailing in their
ship.

“Now, you must cast out the lump of salt”, said the Mastermaid.

So the Prince threw it overboard, and it grew up into a mountain so
high, right across the sea, that the Giant couldn’t pass it, and the
stream-sucker couldn’t help him by swilling any more water.

“Never mind!” cried the Giant; “there’s a cure for this too.” So he
called on his hill-borer to come and bore through the mountain, that
the stream-sucker might creep through and take another swill; but just
as they had made a hole through the hill, and the stream-sucker was
about to drink, the Mastermaid told the Prince to throw overboard a
drop or two out of the flask, and then the sea was just as full as
ever, and before the stream-sucker could take another gulp, they
reached the land and were saved from the Giant.

So they made up their minds to go home to the Prince’s father, but the
Prince would not hear of the Mastermaid’s walking, for he thought it
seemly neither for her nor for him.

“Just wait here ten minutes”, he said, “while I go home after the seven
horses which stand in my father’s stall. It’s no great way off, and I
shan’t be long about it; but I will not hear of my sweetheart walking
to my father’s palace.”

“Ah!” said the Mastermaid, “pray don’t leave me, for if you once get
home to the palace, you’ll forget me outright; I know you will.”

“Oh!” said he, “how can I forget you; you with whom I have gone through
so much, and whom I love so dearly?”

There was no help for it, he must and would go home to fetch the coach
and seven horses, and she was to wait for him by the seaside. So at
last the Mastermaid was forced to let him have his way; she only said:

“Now, when you get home, don’t stop so much as to say good day to any
one, but go straight to the stable and put to the horses, and drive
back as quick as you can; for they will all come about you; but do as
though you did not see them; and above all things, mind you do not
taste a morsel of food, for if you do, we shall both come to grief.”

All this the Prince promised; but he thought all the time there was
little fear of his forgetting her.

Now, just as he came home to the palace, one of his brothers was
thinking of holding his bridal feast, and the bride, and all her kith
and kin, were just come to the palace. So they all thronged round him,
and asked about this thing and that, and wanted him to go in with them;
but he made as though he did not see them, and went straight to the
stall and got out the horses, and began to put them to. And when they
saw they could not get him to go in, they came out to him with meat and
drink, and the best of everything they had got ready for the feast; but
the Prince would not taste so much as a crumb, and put to as fast as he
could. At last the bride’s sister rolled an apple across the yard to
him, saying:

“Well, if you won’t eat anything else, you may as well take a bite of
this, for you must be both hungry and thirsty after so long a journey.”

So he took up the apple and bit a piece out of it; but he had scarce
done so, before he forgot the Mastermaid, and how he was to drive back
for her.

“Well, I think I must be mad”, he said; “what am I to do with this
coach and horses?” So he put the horses up again, and went along with
the others into the palace, and it was soon settled that he should have
the bride’s sister, who had rolled the apple over to him.

There sat the Mastermaid by the seashore, and waited and waited for the
Prince, but no Prince came; so at last she went up from the shore, and
after she had gone a bit she came to a little hut which lay by itself
in a copse close by the king’s palace. She went in and asked if she
might lodge there. It was an old dame that owned the hut, and a
cross-grained scolding hag she was as ever you saw. At first she would
not hear of the Mastermaid’s lodging in her house, but at last, for
fair words and high rent, the Mastermaid got leave to be there. Now the
but was as dark and dirty as a pigsty, so the Mastermaid said she would
smarten it up a little, that their house might look inside like other
people’s. The old hag did not like this either, and showed her teeth,
and was cross; but the Mastermaid did not mind her. She took her chest
of gold, and threw a handful or so into the fire, and lo! the gold
melted, and bubbled and boiled over out of the grate, and spread itself
over the whole hut, till it was gilded both outside and in. But as soon
as the gold began to bubble and boil, the old hag got so afraid that
she tried to run out as if the Evil One were at her heels; and as she
ran out at the door, she forgot to stoop, and gave her head such a
knock against the lintel, that she broke her neck, and that was the end
of her.

Next morning the Constable passed that way, and you may fancy he could
scarce believe his eyes when he saw the golden hut shining and
glistening away in the copse; but he was still more astonished when he
went in and saw the lovely maiden who sat there. To make a long story
short, he fell over head and ears in love with her, and begged and
prayed her to become his wife.

“Well, but have you much money?” asked the Mastermaid.

Yes, for that matter, he said, he was not so badly off, and off he went
home to fetch the money, and when he came back at even he brought a
half-bushel sack, and set it down on the bench. So the Mastermaid said
she would have him, since he was so rich; but they were scarce in bed
before she said she must get up again:

“For I have forgotten to make up the fire.”

“Pray, don’t stir out of bed”, said the Constable; “I’ll see to it.”

So he jumped out of bed, and stood on the hearth in a trice.

“As soon as you have got hold of the shovel, just tell me”, said the
Mastermaid.

“Well, I am holding it now”, said the Constable.

Then the Mastermaid said:

“God grant that you may hold the shovel, and the shovel you, and may
you heap hot burning coals over yourself till morning breaks.”

So there stood the Constable all night long, shovelling hot burning
coals over himself; and though he begged, and prayed, and wept, the
coals were not a bit colder for that; but as soon as day broke, and he
had power to cast away the shovel, he did not stay long, as you may
fancy, but set off as if the Evil One or the bailiff were at his heels;
and all who met him stared their eyes out at him, for he cut capers as
though he were mad, and he could not have looked in worse plight if he
had been flayed and tanned, and every one wondered what had befallen
him, but he told no one where he had been, for shame’s sake.

Next day the Attorney passed by the place where the Mastermaid lived,
and he too saw how it shone and glistened in the copse; so he turned
aside to find out who owned the hut; and when he came in and saw the
lovely maiden, he fell more in love with her than the Constable, and
began to woo her in hot haste.

Well, the Mastermaid asked him, as she had asked the Constable, if he
had a good lot of money? and the Attorney said he wasn’t so badly off;
and as a proof he went home to fetch his money. So at even he came back
with a great fat sack of money—I think it was a whole bushel sack—and
set it down on the bench; and the long and the short of the matter was,
that he was to have her, and they went to bed. But all at once the
Mastermaid had forgotten to shut the door of the porch, and she must
get up and make it fast for the night.

“What, you do that!” said the Attorney, “while I lie here; that can
never be; lie still, while I go and do it.”

So up he jumped, like a pea on a drum-head, and ran out into the porch.

“Tell me”, said the Mastermaid, “when you have hold of the door-latch.”

“I’ve got hold of it now”, said the Attorney.

“God grant, then”, said the Mastermaid, “that you may hold the door,
and the door you, and that you may go from wall to wall till day
dawns.”

So you may fancy what a dance the Attorney had all night long; such a
waltz he never had before, and I don’t think he would much care if he
never had such a waltz again. Now he pulled the door forward, and then
the door pulled him back, and so he went on, now dashed into one corner
of the porch, and now into the other, till he was almost battered to
death. At first he began to curse and swear, and then to beg and pray,
but the door cared for nothing but holding its own till break of day.
As soon as it let go its hold, off set the Attorney, leaving behind him
his money to pay for his night’s lodging, and forgetting his courtship
altogether, for to tell the truth, he was afraid lest the house-door
should come dancing after him. All who met him stared and gaped at him,
for he too cut capers like a madman, and he could not have looked in
worse plight if he had spent the whole night in butting against a flock
of rams.

The third day the Sheriff passed that way, and he too saw the golden
hut, and turned aside to find out who lived there; and he had scarce
set eyes on the Mastermaid, before he began to woo her. So she answered
him as she had answered the other two. If he had lots of money she
would have him, if not, he might go about his business. Well, the
Sheriff said he wasn’t so badly off, and he would go home and fetch the
money, and when he came again at even, he had a bigger sack even than
the Attorney—it must have been at least a bushel and a half, and put it
down on the bench. So it was soon settled that he was to have the
Mastermaid, but they had scarce gone to bed before the Mastermaid said
she had forgotten to bring home the calf from the meadow, so she must
get up and drive him into the stall. Then the Sheriff swore by all the
powers that should never be, and, stout and fat as he was, up he jumped
as nimbly as a kitten.

“Well, only tell me when you’ve got hold of the calf’s tail”, said the
Mastermaid.

“Now I have hold of it”, said the Sheriff.

“God grant”, said the Mastermaid, “that you may hold the calf’s tail,
and the calf’s tail you, and that you may make a tour of the world
together till day dawns”.

Well you may just fancy how the Sheriff had to stretch his legs; away
they went, the calf and he, over high and low, across hill and dale,
and the more the Sheriff cursed and swore, the faster the calf ran and
jumped. At dawn of day the poor Sheriff was well nigh broken-winded,
and so glad was he to let go the calf’s tail, that he forgot his sack
of money and everything else. As he was a great man, he went a little
slower than the Attorney and the Constable, but the slower he went the
more time people had to gape and stare at him; and I must say they made
good use of their time, for he was terribly tattered and torn, after
his dance with the calf.

Next day was fixed for the wedding at the palace, and the eldest
brother was to drive to church with his bride, and the younger, who had
lived with the Giant, with the bride’s sister. But when they had got
into the coach, and were just going to drive off, one of the trace-pins
snapped off; and though they made at least three in its place, they all
broke, from whatever sort of wood they were made. So time went on and
on, and they couldn’t get to church, and every one grew very downcast.
But all at once the Constable said, for he too was bidden to the
wedding, that yonder away in the copse lived a maiden.

“And if you can only get her to lend you the handle of her shovel with
which she makes up her fire, I know very well it will hold.”

Well! they sent a messenger on the spot, with such a pretty message to
the maiden, to know if they couldn’t get the loan of her shovel which
the Constable had spoken of; and the maiden said “yes”, they might have
it; so they got a trace-pin which wasn’t likely to snap.

But all at once, just as they were driving off, the bottom of the coach
tumbled to bits. So they set to work to make a new bottom as they best
might; but it mattered not how many nails they put into it, nor of what
wood they made it, for as soon as ever they got the bottom well into
the coach and were driving off, snap it went in two again, and they
were even worse off than when they lost the trace-pin. Just then the
Attorney said—for if the Constable was there, you may fancy the
Attorney was there too: “Away yonder, in the copse, lives a maiden, and
if you could only get her to lend you one-half of her porch-door, I
know it can hold together.”

Well! they sent another message to the copse, and asked so prettily if
they couldn’t have the loan of the gilded porch-door which the Attorney
had talked of; and they got it on the spot. So they were just setting
out; but now the horses were not strong enough to draw the coach,
though there were six of them; then they put on eight, and ten, and
twelve, but the more they put on, and the more the coachman whipped,
the more the coach wouldn’t stir an inch. By this time it was far on in
the day, and every one about the palace was in doleful dumps; for to
church they must go, and yet it looked as if they should never get
there. So at last the Sheriff said, that yonder in the gilded hut, in
the copse, lived a maiden, and if they could only get the loan of her
calf:

“I know it can drag the coach, though it were as heavy as a mountain.”

Well they all thought it would look silly to be drawn to church by a
calf, but there was no help for it, so they had to send a third time,
and ask so prettily in the King’s name, if he couldn’t get the loan of
the calf the Sheriff had spoken of, and the Mastermaid let them have it
on the spot, for she was not going to say “no” this time either. So
they put the calf on before the horses, and waited to see if it would
do any good, and away went the coach over high and low, and stock and
stone, so that they could scarce draw their breath; sometimes they were
on the ground, and sometimes up in the air, and when they reached the
church, the calf began to run round and round it like a spinning jenny,
so that they had hard work to get out of the coach, and into the
church. When they went back, it was the same story, only they went
faster, and they reached the palace almost before they knew they had
set out.

Now when they sat down to dinner, the Prince who had served with the
Giant said he thought they ought to ask the maiden who had lent them
her shovel-handle and porch-door, and calf, to come up to the palace.

“For”, said he, “if we hadn’t got these three things, we should have
been sticking here still.”

Yes; the King thought that only fair and right, so he sent five of his
best men down to the gilded but to greet the maiden from the King, and
to ask her if she wouldn’t be so good as to came up and dine at the
palace.

“Greet the King from me”, said the Mastermaid, “and tell him, if he’s
too good to come to me, so am I too good to go to him.”

So the King had to go himself, and then the Mastermaid went up with him
without more ado; and as the King thought she was more than she seemed
to be, he sat her down in the highest seat by the side of the youngest
bridegroom.

Now, when they had sat a little while at table, the Mastermaid took out
her golden apple, and the golden cock and hen, which she had carried
off from the Giant, and put them down on the table before her, and the
cock and hen began at once to peck at one another, and to fight for the
golden apple.

“Oh! only look”, said the Prince; “see how those two strive for the
apple.”

“Yes!” said the Mastermaid; “so we two strove to get away that time
when we were together in the hillside.”

Then the spell was broken, and the Prince knew her again, and you may
fancy how glad he was. But as for the witch who had rolled the apple
over to him, he had her torn to pieces between twenty-four horses, so
that there was not a bit of her left, and after that they held on with
the wedding in real earnest; and though they were still stiff and
footsore, the Constable, the Attorney, and the Sheriff, kept it up with
the best of them.
paragraphs: Once on a time there was a king who had several sons—I don’t know how many there were—but the youngest had no rest at home, for nothing else would please him but to go out into the world and try his luck, and after a long time the king was forced to give him leave to go. Now, after he had travelled some days, he came one night to a Giant’s house, and there he got a place in the Giant’s service. In the morning the Giant went off to herd his goats, and as he left the yard, he told the Prince to clean out the stable; “and after you have done that, you needn’t do anything else to-day; for you must know it is an easy master you have come to. But what is set you to do you must do well, and you mustn’t think of going into any of the rooms which are beyond that in which you slept, for if you do, I’ll take your life.”
“Sure enough, it is an easy master I have got”, said the Prince to himself, as he walked up and down the room, and carolled and sang, for he thought there was plenty of time to clean out the stable.
“But still it would be good fun just to peep into his other rooms, for there must be something in them which he is afraid lest I should see, since he won’t give me leave to go in.”

So he went into the first room, and there was a pot boiling on a hook by the wall, but the Prince saw no fire underneath it. I wonder what is inside it, he thought; and then he dipped a lock of his hair into it, and the hair seemed as if it were all turned to copper.

“What a dainty broth,” he said; “if one tasted it, he’d look grand inside his gullet”; and with that he went into the next room. There, too, was a pot hanging by a hook, which bubbled and boiled; but there was no fire under that either.
“I may as well try this too”, said the Prince, as he put another lock into the pot, and it came out all silvered.

“They haven’t such rich broth in my father’s house”, said the Prince; “but it all depends on how it tastes”, and with that he went on into the third room. There, too, hung a pot, and boiled just as he had seen in the two other rooms, and the Prince had a mind to try this too, so he dipped a lock of hair into it, and it came out gilded, so that the light gleamed from it.
“‘Worse and worse’, said the old wife; but I say better and better”, said the Prince; “but if he boils gold here, I wonder what he boils in yonder.”

He thought he might as well see; so he went through the door into the fourth room. Well, there was no pot in there, but there was a Princess, seated on a bench, so lovely, that the Prince had never seen anything like her in his born days.
“Oh! in Heaven’s name”, she said, “what do you want here?”
“I got a place here yesterday”, said the Prince.
“A place, indeed! Heaven help you out of it.”
“Well, after all, I think I’ve got an easy master; he hasn’t set me much to do to-day, for after I have cleaned out the stable, my day’s work is over.”

“Yes, but how will you do it”, she said; “for if you set to work to clean it like other folk, ten pitchforks full will come in for every one you toss out. But I will teach you how to set to work; you must turn the fork upside down, and toss with the handle, and then all the dung will fly out of itself.”

“Yes, he would be sure to do that”, said the Prince; and so he sat there the whole day, for he and the Princess were soon great friends, and had made up their minds to have one another, and so the first day of his service with the Giant was not long, you may fancy. But when the evening drew on, she said “twould be as well if he got the stable cleaned out before the Giant came home; and when he went to the stable, he thought he would just see if what she had said were true, and so he began to work like the grooms in his father’s stable; but he soon had enough of that, for he hadn’t worked a minute before the stable was so full of dung that he hadn’t room to stand. Then he did as the Princess bade him, and turned up the fork and worked with the handle, and lo! in a trice the stable was as clean as if it had been scoured. And when he had done his work, he went back into the room where the Giant had given him leave to be, and began to walk up and down, and to carol and sing. So after a bit, home came the Giant with his goats.
“Have you cleaned the stable?” asked the Giant.
“Yes, now it’s all right and tight, master”, answered the Prince.
“I’ll soon see if it is”, growled the Giant, and strode off to the stable, where he found it just as the Prince had said.
“You’ve been talking to my Mastermaid, I can see”, said the Giant; “for you’ve not sucked this knowledge out of your own breast.”
“Mastermaid!” said the Prince, who looked as stupid as an owl, “what sort of thing is that, master? I’d be very glad to see it.”
“Well, well!” said the Giant; “you’ll see her soon enough”.

Next day the Giant set off with his goats again, and before he went he told the Prince to fetch home his horse, which was out at grass on the hill-side, and when he had done that he might rest all the day.
“For you must know, it is an easy master you have come to”, said the Giant; “but if you go into any of the rooms I spoke of yesterday, I’ll wring your head off.”
So off he went with his flock of goats.

“An easy master you are indeed”, said the Prince; “but for all that, I’ll just go in and have a chat with your Mastermaid; may be she’ll be as soon mine as yours.” So he went in to her, and she asked him what he had to do that day.
“Oh! nothing to be afraid of”, said he; “I’ve only to go up to the hill-side to fetch his horse.”
“Very well, and how will you set about it?”
“Well, for that matter, there’s no great art in riding a horse home. I fancy I’ve ridden fresher horses before now”, said the Prince.

“Ah, but this isn’t so easy a task as you think; but I’ll teach you how to do it. When you get near it, fire and flame will come out of its nostrils, as out of a tar barrel; but look out, and take the bit which hangs behind the door yonder, and throw it right into his jaws, and he will grow so tame that you may do what you like with him.”

Yes! the Prince would mind and do that; and so he sat in there the whole day, talking and chattering with the Mastermaid about one thing and another, but they always came back to how happy they would be if they could only have one another, and get well away from the Giant; and, to tell the truth, the Prince would have clean forgotten both the horse and the hill-side, if the Mastermaid hadn’t put him in mind of them when evening drew on, telling him he had better set out to fetch the horse before the Giant came home. So he set off, and took the bit which hung in the corner, ran up the hill, and it wasn’t long before he met the horse, with fire and flame streaming out of its nostrils. But he watched his time, and, as the horse came open-jawed up to him, he threw the bit into its mouth, and it stood as quiet as a lamb. After that, it was no great matter to ride it home and put it up, you may fancy; and then the Prince went into his room again, and began to carol and sing.
So the Giant came home again at even with his goats; and the first words he said were:
“Have you brought my horse down from the hill?”
“Yes, master, that I have”, said the Prince; “and a better horse I never bestrode; but for all that I rode him straight home, and put him up safe and sound.”
“I’ll soon see to that”, said the Giant, and ran out to the stable, and there stood the horse just as the Prince had said.
“You’ve talked to my Mastermaid, I’ll be bound, for you haven’t sucked this out of your own breast”, said the Giant again.

“Yesterday master talked of this Mastermaid, and to-day it’s the same story”, said the Prince, who pretended to be silly and stupid. “Bless you, master! why don’t you show me the thing at once? I should so like to see it only once in my life.”
“Oh, if that’s all”, said the Giant, “you’ll see her soon enough.”
The third day, at dawn, the Giant went off to the wood again with his goats; but before he went he said to the Prince:
“To-day you must go to Hell and fetch my fire-tax. When you have done that you can rest yourself all day, for you must know it is an easy master you have come to”; and with that off he went.

“Easy master, indeed!” said the Prince. “You may be easy, but you set me hard tasks all the same. But I may as well see if I can find your Mastermaid, as you call her. I daresay she’ll tell me what to do”; and so in he went to her again.
So when the Mastermaid asked what the Giant had set him to do that day, he told her how he was to go to Hell and fetch the fire-tax.
“And how will you set about it?” asked the Mastermaid.
“Oh, that you must tell me”, said the Prince. “I have never been to Hell in my life; and even if I knew the way, I don’t know how much I am to ask for.”

“Well, I’ll soon tell you”, said the Mastermaid; “you must go to the steep rock away yonder, under the hill-side, and take the club that lies there, and knock on the face of the rock. Then there will come out one all glistening with fire; to him you must tell your errand; and when he asks you how much you will have, mind you say, ‘As much as I can carry.’”

Yes; he would be sure to say that; so he sat in there with the Mastermaid all that day too; and though evening drew on, he would have sat there till now, had not the Mastermaid put him in mind that it was high time to be off to Hell to fetch the Giant’s fire-tax before he came home. So he went on his way, and did just as the Mastermaid had told him; and when he reached the rock, he took up the club and gave a great thump. Then the rock opened, and out came one whose face glistened, and out of whose eyes and nostrils flew sparks of fire.
“What is your will?” said he.
“Oh! I’m only come from the Giant to fetch his fire-tax”, said the Prince.
“How much will you have then?” said the other.
“I never wish for more than I am able to carry”, said the Prince.
“Lucky for you that you did not ask for a whole horse-load”, said he who came out of the rock; “but come now into the rock with me, and you shall have it.”

So the Prince went in with him, and you may fancy what heaps and heaps of gold and silver he saw lying in there, just like stones in a gravel pit; and he got a load just as big as he was able to carry, and set off home with it. Now, when the Giant came home with his goats at even, the Prince went into his room, and began to carol and sing as he had done the evenings before.
“Have you been to Hell after my fire-tax?” roared the Giant.
“Oh yes; that I have, master”, answered the Prince.
“Where have you put it?” said the Giant.
“There stands the sack on the bench yonder”, said the Prince.
“I’ll soon see to that”, said the Giant, who strode off to the bench, and there he saw the sack so full that the gold and silver dropped out on the floor as soon as ever he untied the string.
“You’ve been talking to my Mastermaid, that I can see”, said the Giant; “but if you have, I’ll wring your head off.”

“Mastermaid!” said the Prince; “yesterday master talked of this Mastermaid, and to-day he talks of her again, and the day before yesterday it was the same story. I only wish I could see what sort of thing she is! that I do.”
“Well, well, wait till to-morrow”, said the Giant, “and then I’ll take you in to her myself.”
“Thank you kindly, master”, said the Prince; “but it’s only a joke of master’s, I’ll be bound.”
So next day the Giant took him in to the Mastermaid, and said to her:
“Now, you must cut his throat, and boil him in the great big pot you wot of; and when the broth is ready, just give me a call.”
After that, he laid him down on the bench to sleep, and began to snore so, that it sounded like thunder on the hills.

So the Mastermaid took a knife and cut the Prince in his little finger, and let three drops of blood fall on a three-legged stool; and after that she took all the old rags, and soles of shoes, and all the rubbish she could lay hands on, and put them into the pot; and then she filled a chest full of ground gold, and took a lump of salt, and a flask of water that hung behind the door, and she took, besides, a golden apple, and two golden chickens, and off she set with the Prince from the Giant’s house as fast as they could; and when they had gone a little way, they came to the sea, and after that they sailed over the sea; but where they got the ship from, I have never heard tell.
So when the Giant had slumbered a good bit, he began to stretch himself as he lay on the bench and called out, “Will it be soon done?”
“Only just begun”, answered the first drop of blood on the stool.
So the Giant lay down to sleep again, and slumbered a long, long time. At last he began to toss about a little, and cried out:
“Do you hear what I say; will it be soon done?” but he did not look up this time, any more than the first, for he was still half asleep.
“Half done”, said the second drop of blood.

Then the Giant thought again it was the Mastermaid, so he turned over on his other side, and fell asleep again; and when he had gone on sleeping for many hours, he began to stir and stretch his old bones, and to call out,—
“Isn’t it done yet?”
“Done to a turn”, said the third drop of blood.
Then the Giant rose up and began to rub his eyes, but he couldn’t see who it was that was talking to him, so he searched and called for the Mastermaid, but no one answered.

“Ah, well! I dare say she’s just run out of doors for a bit”, he thought, and took up a spoon and went up to the pot to taste the broth; but he found nothing but shoe-soles, and rags, and such stuff; and it was all boiled up together, so that he couldn’t tell which was thick and which was thin. As soon as he saw this, he could tell how things had gone, and he got so angry he scarce knew which leg to stand upon. Away he went after the Prince and the Mastermaid, till the wind whistled behind him; but before long, he came to the water and couldn’t cross it.
“Never mind”, he said; “I know a cure for this. I’ve only got to call on my stream-sucker.”

So he called on his stream-sucker, and he came and stooped down, and took one, two, three gulps; and then the water fell so much in the sea, that the Giant could see the Mastermaid and the Prince sailing in their ship.
“Now, you must cast out the lump of salt”, said the Mastermaid.
So the Prince threw it overboard, and it grew up into a mountain so high, right across the sea, that the Giant couldn’t pass it, and the stream-sucker couldn’t help him by swilling any more water.

“Never mind!” cried the Giant; “there’s a cure for this too.” So he called on his hill-borer to come and bore through the mountain, that the stream-sucker might creep through and take another swill; but just as they had made a hole through the hill, and the stream-sucker was about to drink, the Mastermaid told the Prince to throw overboard a drop or two out of the flask, and then the sea was just as full as ever, and before the stream-sucker could take another gulp, they reached the land and were saved from the Giant.
So they made up their minds to go home to the Prince’s father, but the Prince would not hear of the Mastermaid’s walking, for he thought it seemly neither for her nor for him.

“Just wait here ten minutes”, he said, “while I go home after the seven horses which stand in my father’s stall. It’s no great way off, and I shan’t be long about it; but I will not hear of my sweetheart walking to my father’s palace.”
“Ah!” said the Mastermaid, “pray don’t leave me, for if you once get home to the palace, you’ll forget me outright; I know you will.”
“Oh!” said he, “how can I forget you; you with whom I have gone through so much, and whom I love so dearly?”

There was no help for it, he must and would go home to fetch the coach and seven horses, and she was to wait for him by the seaside. So at last the Mastermaid was forced to let him have his way; she only said:

“Now, when you get home, don’t stop so much as to say good day to any one, but go straight to the stable and put to the horses, and drive back as quick as you can; for they will all come about you; but do as though you did not see them; and above all things, mind you do not taste a morsel of food, for if you do, we shall both come to grief.”
All this the Prince promised; but he thought all the time there was little fear of his forgetting her.

Now, just as he came home to the palace, one of his brothers was thinking of holding his bridal feast, and the bride, and all her kith and kin, were just come to the palace. So they all thronged round him, and asked about this thing and that, and wanted him to go in with them; but he made as though he did not see them, and went straight to the stall and got out the horses, and began to put them to. And when they saw they could not get him to go in, they came out to him with meat and drink, and the best of everything they had got ready for the feast; but the Prince would not taste so much as a crumb, and put to as fast as he could. At last the bride’s sister rolled an apple across the yard to him, saying:
“Well, if you won’t eat anything else, you may as well take a bite of this, for you must be both hungry and thirsty after so long a journey.”
So he took up the apple and bit a piece out of it; but he had scarce done so, before he forgot the Mastermaid, and how he was to drive back for her.

“Well, I think I must be mad”, he said; “what am I to do with this coach and horses?” So he put the horses up again, and went along with the others into the palace, and it was soon settled that he should have the bride’s sister, who had rolled the apple over to him.

There sat the Mastermaid by the seashore, and waited and waited for the Prince, but no Prince came; so at last she went up from the shore, and after she had gone a bit she came to a little hut which lay by itself in a copse close by the king’s palace. She went in and asked if she might lodge there. It was an old dame that owned the hut, and a cross-grained scolding hag she was as ever you saw. At first she would not hear of the Mastermaid’s lodging in her house, but at last, for fair words and high rent, the Mastermaid got leave to be there. Now the but was as dark and dirty as a pigsty, so the Mastermaid said she would smarten it up a little, that their house might look inside like other people’s. The old hag did not like this either, and showed her teeth, and was cross; but the Mastermaid did not mind her. She took her chest of gold, and threw a handful or so into the fire, and lo! the gold melted, and bubbled and boiled over out of the grate, and spread itself over the whole hut, till it was gilded both outside and in. But as soon as the gold began to bubble and boil, the old hag got so afraid that she tried to run out as if the Evil One were at her heels; and as she ran out at the door, she forgot to stoop, and gave her head such a knock against the lintel, that she broke her neck, and that was the end of her.

Next morning the Constable passed that way, and you may fancy he could scarce believe his eyes when he saw the golden hut shining and glistening away in the copse; but he was still more astonished when he went in and saw the lovely maiden who sat there. To make a long story short, he fell over head and ears in love with her, and begged and prayed her to become his wife.
“Well, but have you much money?” asked the Mastermaid.

Yes, for that matter, he said, he was not so badly off, and off he went home to fetch the money, and when he came back at even he brought a half-bushel sack, and set it down on the bench. So the Mastermaid said she would have him, since he was so rich; but they were scarce in bed before she said she must get up again:
“For I have forgotten to make up the fire.”
“Pray, don’t stir out of bed”, said the Constable; “I’ll see to it.”
So he jumped out of bed, and stood on the hearth in a trice.
“As soon as you have got hold of the shovel, just tell me”, said the Mastermaid.
“Well, I am holding it now”, said the Constable.
Then the Mastermaid said:
“God grant that you may hold the shovel, and the shovel you, and may you heap hot burning coals over yourself till morning breaks.”

So there stood the Constable all night long, shovelling hot burning coals over himself; and though he begged, and prayed, and wept, the coals were not a bit colder for that; but as soon as day broke, and he had power to cast away the shovel, he did not stay long, as you may fancy, but set off as if the Evil One or the bailiff were at his heels; and all who met him stared their eyes out at him, for he cut capers as though he were mad, and he could not have looked in worse plight if he had been flayed and tanned, and every one wondered what had befallen him, but he told no one where he had been, for shame’s sake.

Next day the Attorney passed by the place where the Mastermaid lived, and he too saw how it shone and glistened in the copse; so he turned aside to find out who owned the hut; and when he came in and saw the lovely maiden, he fell more in love with her than the Constable, and began to woo her in hot haste.

Well, the Mastermaid asked him, as she had asked the Constable, if he had a good lot of money? and the Attorney said he wasn’t so badly off; and as a proof he went home to fetch his money. So at even he came back with a great fat sack of money—I think it was a whole bushel sack—and set it down on the bench; and the long and the short of the matter was, that he was to have her, and they went to bed. But all at once the Mastermaid had forgotten to shut the door of the porch, and she must get up and make it fast for the night.
“What, you do that!” said the Attorney, “while I lie here; that can never be; lie still, while I go and do it.”
So up he jumped, like a pea on a drum-head, and ran out into the porch.
“Tell me”, said the Mastermaid, “when you have hold of the door-latch.”
“I’ve got hold of it now”, said the Attorney.
“God grant, then”, said the Mastermaid, “that you may hold the door, and the door you, and that you may go from wall to wall till day dawns.”

So you may fancy what a dance the Attorney had all night long; such a waltz he never had before, and I don’t think he would much care if he never had such a waltz again. Now he pulled the door forward, and then the door pulled him back, and so he went on, now dashed into one corner of the porch, and now into the other, till he was almost battered to death. At first he began to curse and swear, and then to beg and pray, but the door cared for nothing but holding its own till break of day. As soon as it let go its hold, off set the Attorney, leaving behind him his money to pay for his night’s lodging, and forgetting his courtship altogether, for to tell the truth, he was afraid lest the house-door should come dancing after him. All who met him stared and gaped at him, for he too cut capers like a madman, and he could not have looked in worse plight if he had spent the whole night in butting against a flock of rams.

The third day the Sheriff passed that way, and he too saw the golden hut, and turned aside to find out who lived there; and he had scarce set eyes on the Mastermaid, before he began to woo her. So she answered him as she had answered the other two. If he had lots of money she would have him, if not, he might go about his business. Well, the Sheriff said he wasn’t so badly off, and he would go home and fetch the money, and when he came again at even, he had a bigger sack even than the Attorney—it must have been at least a bushel and a half, and put it down on the bench. So it was soon settled that he was to have the Mastermaid, but they had scarce gone to bed before the Mastermaid said she had forgotten to bring home the calf from the meadow, so she must get up and drive him into the stall. Then the Sheriff swore by all the powers that should never be, and, stout and fat as he was, up he jumped as nimbly as a kitten.
“Well, only tell me when you’ve got hold of the calf’s tail”, said the Mastermaid.
“Now I have hold of it”, said the Sheriff.
“God grant”, said the Mastermaid, “that you may hold the calf’s tail, and the calf’s tail you, and that you may make a tour of the world together till day dawns”.

Well you may just fancy how the Sheriff had to stretch his legs; away they went, the calf and he, over high and low, across hill and dale, and the more the Sheriff cursed and swore, the faster the calf ran and jumped. At dawn of day the poor Sheriff was well nigh broken-winded, and so glad was he to let go the calf’s tail, that he forgot his sack of money and everything else. As he was a great man, he went a little slower than the Attorney and the Constable, but the slower he went the more time people had to gape and stare at him; and I must say they made good use of their time, for he was terribly tattered and torn, after his dance with the calf.

Next day was fixed for the wedding at the palace, and the eldest brother was to drive to church with his bride, and the younger, who had lived with the Giant, with the bride’s sister. But when they had got into the coach, and were just going to drive off, one of the trace-pins snapped off; and though they made at least three in its place, they all broke, from whatever sort of wood they were made. So time went on and on, and they couldn’t get to church, and every one grew very downcast. But all at once the Constable said, for he too was bidden to the wedding, that yonder away in the copse lived a maiden.
“And if you can only get her to lend you the handle of her shovel with which she makes up her fire, I know very well it will hold.”

Well! they sent a messenger on the spot, with such a pretty message to the maiden, to know if they couldn’t get the loan of her shovel which the Constable had spoken of; and the maiden said “yes”, they might have it; so they got a trace-pin which wasn’t likely to snap.

But all at once, just as they were driving off, the bottom of the coach tumbled to bits. So they set to work to make a new bottom as they best might; but it mattered not how many nails they put into it, nor of what wood they made it, for as soon as ever they got the bottom well into the coach and were driving off, snap it went in two again, and they were even worse off than when they lost the trace-pin. Just then the Attorney said—for if the Constable was there, you may fancy the Attorney was there too: “Away yonder, in the copse, lives a maiden, and if you could only get her to lend you one-half of her porch-door, I know it can hold together.”

Well! they sent another message to the copse, and asked so prettily if they couldn’t have the loan of the gilded porch-door which the Attorney had talked of; and they got it on the spot. So they were just setting out; but now the horses were not strong enough to draw the coach, though there were six of them; then they put on eight, and ten, and twelve, but the more they put on, and the more the coachman whipped, the more the coach wouldn’t stir an inch. By this time it was far on in the day, and every one about the palace was in doleful dumps; for to church they must go, and yet it looked as if they should never get there. So at last the Sheriff said, that yonder in the gilded hut, in the copse, lived a maiden, and if they could only get the loan of her calf:
“I know it can drag the coach, though it were as heavy as a mountain.”

Well they all thought it would look silly to be drawn to church by a calf, but there was no help for it, so they had to send a third time, and ask so prettily in the King’s name, if he couldn’t get the loan of the calf the Sheriff had spoken of, and the Mastermaid let them have it on the spot, for she was not going to say “no” this time either. So they put the calf on before the horses, and waited to see if it would do any good, and away went the coach over high and low, and stock and stone, so that they could scarce draw their breath; sometimes they were on the ground, and sometimes up in the air, and when they reached the church, the calf began to run round and round it like a spinning jenny, so that they had hard work to get out of the coach, and into the church. When they went back, it was the same story, only they went faster, and they reached the palace almost before they knew they had set out.

Now when they sat down to dinner, the Prince who had served with the Giant said he thought they ought to ask the maiden who had lent them her shovel-handle and porch-door, and calf, to come up to the palace.
“For”, said he, “if we hadn’t got these three things, we should have been sticking here still.”

Yes; the King thought that only fair and right, so he sent five of his best men down to the gilded but to greet the maiden from the King, and to ask her if she wouldn’t be so good as to came up and dine at the palace.
“Greet the King from me”, said the Mastermaid, “and tell him, if he’s too good to come to me, so am I too good to go to him.”

So the King had to go himself, and then the Mastermaid went up with him without more ado; and as the King thought she was more than she seemed to be, he sat her down in the highest seat by the side of the youngest bridegroom.

Now, when they had sat a little while at table, the Mastermaid took out her golden apple, and the golden cock and hen, which she had carried off from the Giant, and put them down on the table before her, and the cock and hen began at once to peck at one another, and to fight for the golden apple.
“Oh! only look”, said the Prince; “see how those two strive for the apple.”
“Yes!” said the Mastermaid; “so we two strove to get away that time when we were together in the hillside.”

Then the spell was broken, and the Prince knew her again, and you may fancy how glad he was. But as for the witch who had rolled the apple over to him, he had her torn to pieces between twenty-four horses, so that there was not a bit of her left, and after that they held on with the wedding in real earnest; and though they were still stiff and footsore, the Constable, the Attorney, and the Sheriff, kept it up with the best of them.

むかしむかし、一人の王に何人もの息子がいた——何人いたかは知らない——だが末の息子は家にいても落ち着かず、世に出て運を試すことのほかは何も気に入らなかった。そして長いことかかって、王は行く許しを与えざるを得なくなった。さて幾日か旅をしたあと、ある夜、彼は巨人の家に着き、そこで巨人に仕える口を得た。朝になると巨人は山羊を追って出かけていったが、庭を出るとき王子に厩を掃除せよと言いつけた。「それを済ませたら、今日はほかに何もしなくてよい。おまえが来たのは楽な主人のところだと知るがいい。だが言いつけられたことはきちんとやらねばならん。それから、おまえが寝た部屋より奥の部屋には、どれ一つ入ろうなどと考えるな。入ったら命をもらうぞ。」
「なるほど、楽な主人のところへ来たものだ」と王子はひとりごちながら部屋を行ったり来たりして、歌をうたい鼻歌を歌った。厩を掃除する時間はたっぷりあると思ったのである。
「だがそれでも、ほかの部屋をのぞいてみるのは面白かろう。入る許しをくれないからには、見られたくない何かがあるに違いない。」
そこで彼は最初の部屋に入った。するとそこには壁の鉤に掛けた鍋が煮えていたが、その下に火は見えなかった。何が入っているのだろう、と彼は思った。そして自分の髪をひと房そこへ浸してみると、髪はすっかり銅に変わったように見えた。
「なんとうまそうなスープだ」と彼は言った。「これを味わったら、喉のなかまで立派になるだろう。」。そう言って隣の部屋へ入った。そこにもまた鉤に掛けた鍋があって、ぶくぶくと煮えていた。だがその下にも火はなかった。
「これも試してみるか」と王子は言って、もうひと房を鍋に浸した。すると髪はすっかり銀色になって出てきた。
「父の家にもこんな豪勢なスープはないな」と王子は言った。「だが何もかも味しだいだ。」。そう言って三つめの部屋へ進んだ。そこにも鍋が掛かっていて、ほかの二つの部屋で見たのと同じように煮えていた。そして王子はこれも試してみる気になって髪をひと房浸してみると、それは金めっきされて出てきて、光がきらめくほどだった。
「『悪くなる一方だ』と婆さんは言ったが、わたしは言おう、よくなる一方だと」と王子は言った。「だがここで黄金を煮ているなら、向こうでは何を煮ているのだろう。」
見ておいてもよかろうと思って、彼は戸を抜けて四つめの部屋へ入った。さて、そこには鍋はなかったが、腰掛けに坐った姫が一人いた。あまりに美しくて、王子は生まれてこのかたこんな人を見たことがなかった。
「まあ! 後生ですから」と姫は言った。「ここで何をしているのです。」
「昨日ここに仕える口を得たのです」と王子は言った。
「仕える口ですって! 天があなたをそこから救い出してくださいますように。」
「なに、それでもわたしは楽な主人にあたったと思いますよ。今日はあまり言いつけられていない。厩を掃除したら、一日の仕事はおしまいです。」
「ええ、でもどうやってやるのです」と姫は言った。「ほかの人たちのように掃除にかかったら、一杯放り出すごとに熊手十杯分が入ってくるのです。でもやり方を教えてあげましょう。熊手を逆さまにして、柄のほうで放るのです。そうすれば糞はひとりでにみな飛び出していきます。」

「ええ、きっとそうしましょう」と王子は言った。そうして彼は一日じゅうそこに坐っていた。彼と姫はたちまち仲よくなり、たがいを連れ合いにしようと心を決めていたのである。だから巨人に仕えた最初の一日は長くなかった、それはお察しのとおりである。だが夕方が近づくと姫は、巨人が帰ってくる前に厩を掃除しておくほうがよいと言った。そして厩へ行くと、彼は姫の言ったことが本当かどうか見てやろうと思って、父の厩の馬丁たちのようにやりはじめた。だがすぐにうんざりした。一分も働かぬうちに厩は糞でいっぱいになって、立つ場所もなくなったのである。そこで姫に言われたとおり熊手を逆さにして柄で働いた。すると見よ! たちまち厩は磨き上げたようにきれいになった。そして仕事を終えると、巨人が居てもよいと言った部屋へ戻り、行ったり来たりしながら歌をうたい鼻歌を歌いはじめた。そうしてしばらくすると、巨人が山羊を連れて帰ってきた。
「厩は掃除したか」と巨人は尋ねた。
「はい、いまはすっかり片づいております、ご主人」と王子は答えた。
「すぐに確かめてやる」と巨人は唸って、大股で厩へ行った。すると王子の言ったとおりだった。
「わしの名人娘と話したな、それはわかる」と巨人は言った。「こんな知恵は自分の胸から吸い出せるものではない。」
「名人娘!」と王子は、梟のように間抜けな顔をして言った。「それはどういうものです、ご主人。ぜひ見てみたいものです。」
「まあまあ!」と巨人は言った。「じきに見られるとも。」
翌日、巨人はまた山羊を連れて出かけたが、出かける前に王子に、丘の斜面で草を食んでいる自分の馬を連れ戻してこいと言いつけた。そしてそれが済んだら一日じゅう休んでよい、と。
「おまえが来たのは楽な主人のところだと知るがいい」と巨人は言った。「だが昨日言った部屋のどれかに入ったら、首をねじ切ってやるぞ。」
そうして山羊の群れを連れて出ていった。
「まったく楽な主人だ」と王子は言った。「だがそれでも、ちょっと入ってあんたの名人娘とやらと話してこよう。あんたのものと同じくらい早く、わたしのものになるかもしれん。」。そう言って姫のところへ入っていくと、姫は今日は何をしなければならないのかと尋ねた。
「なに、恐れるほどのことはありません」と彼は言った。「丘の斜面へ行って馬を連れてくるだけです。」
「なるほど、それでどうやってやるつもりですか。」
「なに、それについては、馬に乗って帰るくらいのこと、大した技も要りますまい。もっと元気のいい馬に乗ったこともありますからね」と王子は言った。
「ええ、でもこれはあなたが思うほど楽な務めではありません。でもやり方を教えてあげましょう。近づくと、その鼻孔から瀝青の樽から出るように火と炎が噴き出します。けれど気をつけて、あそこの戸のうしろに掛かっている轡を取って、まっすぐその顎へ投げ込むのです。そうすれば馬はたいそう大人しくなって、好きなようにできます。」

はい! 王子は気をつけてそうしよう、と言った。そうして彼は一日じゅうそこに坐って、名人娘とあれこれ語り合いおしゃべりしていた。だが話はいつも、二人がたがいのものになって巨人からうまく逃れられたらどんなに幸せだろう、というところへ戻るのだった。そして正直に言えば、夕方が近づいて名人娘が思い出させてくれなかったら、王子は馬のことも丘の斜面のことも、きれいさっぱり忘れていたことだろう。姫は、巨人が帰ってくる前に馬を取りに出かけたほうがよいと言った。そこで彼は出かけ、隅に掛かっていた轡を取って丘を駆け上がった。するとまもなく、鼻孔から火と炎を噴き出している馬に出会った。だが彼は頃合いを見計らい、馬が顎を開けて向かってきたところで轡をその口へ投げ込んだ。すると馬は仔羊のように大人しく立った。そのあとは、乗って帰って厩に入れるのは造作もないことだった、それはお察しのとおりである。それから王子はまた自分の部屋へ入って、歌をうたい鼻歌を歌いはじめた。
そうして巨人が夕方に山羊を連れて帰ってきた。そして最初に言った言葉はこうだった。
「丘からわしの馬を連れてきたか。」
「はい、ご主人、連れてまいりました」と王子は言った。「あれほどよい馬にまたがったことはありません。ですがそれでもまっすぐ乗って帰って、無事に厩に入れておきました。」
「すぐに確かめてやる」と巨人は言って厩へ駆け出した。すると王子の言ったとおり馬が立っていた。
「わしの名人娘と話したな、間違いない。こんなことを自分の胸から吸い出せるものではない」と巨人はまた言った。
「昨日もご主人はこの名人娘のことを言われた。そして今日も同じ話だ」と、間抜けで愚かなふりをしている王子は言った。「後生ですよ、ご主人! なぜすぐにそれを見せてくださらないのです。一生に一度でいいから見てみたいものです。」
「なに、それだけのことなら」と巨人は言った。「じきに見られるとも。」
三日め、夜明けに巨人はまた山羊を連れて森へ出かけた。だが出かける前に王子にこう言った。
「今日は地獄へ行って、わしの火の税を取ってこい。それが済んだら一日じゅう休んでよい。おまえが来たのは楽な主人のところだと知るがいい。」。そう言って出ていった。
「まったく楽な主人だ!」と王子は言った。「あんたは楽だろうが、わたしには難儀な務めばかり言いつける。だがまあ、あんたの言う名人娘とやらを見つけられるか試してみよう。どうすればよいか教えてくれるだろう。」。そう言ってまた姫のところへ入っていった。
そこで名人娘が、今日は巨人に何を言いつけられたのかと尋ねると、彼は地獄へ行って火の税を取ってこいと言われたことを話した。
「それでどうやってやるつもりですか」と名人娘は尋ねた。
「なに、それをあなたが教えてくれるのでしょう」と王子は言った。「地獄へなど生まれてこのかた行ったことがない。それに道を知っていたとしても、どれだけもらえばよいのかわからない。」
「では教えてあげましょう」と名人娘は言った。「あちらの丘のふもとの切り立った岩へ行って、そこに置いてある棍棒を取り、岩の面を叩くのです。すると火でぎらぎら輝く者が出てきます。その者に用向きを伝えなさい。そしてどれだけほしいかと訊かれたら、『運べるだけ』と言うのを忘れないように。」

はい、必ずそう言いましょう。そうして彼はその日も一日じゅう名人娘とそこに坐っていた。そして夕方が近づいても、名人娘が、巨人が帰る前に地獄へ火の税を取りに行く時分だと思い出させてくれなかったら、彼はいまでもそこに坐っていたことだろう。そこで彼は出かけ、名人娘に言われたとおりにした。そして岩に着くと棍棒を取り上げて力いっぱい叩いた。すると岩が開いて、顔がぎらぎら輝き、目と鼻孔から火の粉を散らす者が出てきた。
「何の用だ」とその者は言った。
「なに、巨人のところから火の税を取りに来ただけです」と王子は言った。
「ではどれだけほしい」とその者は言った。
「自分で運べる以上は決して望みません」と王子は言った。
「馬一頭分などと言わなかったのは運がよかったな」と岩から出てきた者は言った。「さあ、わたしといっしょに岩のなかへ来い。それを取らせてやろう。」
そこで王子はその者といっしょに入っていった。するとそこに、砂利穴の石ころのように黄金と銀が山と積まれているのを見た。それがどれほどのものだったかはお察しのとおりである。そして彼は運べるだけの荷を受け取って、それを持って家へ帰った。さて巨人が夕方に山羊を連れて帰ってくると、王子は自分の部屋へ入って、前の晩と同じように歌をうたい鼻歌を歌いはじめた。
「わしの火の税を取りに地獄へ行ったか」と巨人は吠えた。
「はい、参りました、ご主人」と王子は答えた。
「どこへ置いた」と巨人は言った。
「あちらの腰掛けの上に袋が置いてあります」と王子は言った。
「すぐに確かめてやる」と巨人は言って腰掛けへ大股で歩いていった。すると袋はぱんぱんで、紐をほどくやいなや黄金と銀が床にこぼれ落ちた。
「わしの名人娘と話したな、それはわかる」と巨人は言った。「だがもしそうなら、首をねじ切ってやるぞ。」
「名人娘!」と王子は言った。「昨日もご主人はこの名人娘のことを言われた。今日もまたその話だ。そして一昨日も同じ話だった。それがどういうものか見られさえすればよいのに! まったくそう思います。」
「まあまあ、明日まで待て」と巨人は言った。「そうしたらわし自身がおまえをそこへ連れていってやる。」
「ありがたいことです、ご主人」と王子は言った。「ですがご主人のご冗談でしょう、きっと。」
そこで翌日、巨人は王子を名人娘のところへ連れていって、娘にこう言った。
「さあ、こいつの喉をかき切って、おまえの知っているあの大きな鍋で煮ろ。そしてスープができたら呼んでくれ。」
そう言って彼は腰掛けに横になって眠り、丘の上の雷のような鼾をかきはじめた。

そこで名人娘は小刀を取って王子の小指を切り、三本脚の床几に血を三滴落とした。そのあと古いぼろと靴底と、手に入るかぎりのがらくたを集めて鍋に入れた。それから櫃いっぱいに砕いた黄金を詰め、塩の塊と、戸のうしろに掛かっていた水の瓶を取り、そのうえ黄金の林檎一つと黄金の雛鶏二羽を取って、王子とともに巨人の家からできるかぎり急いで逃げ出した。そして少し行くと海に出て、そのあと海を渡って船で行った。だが船をどこで手に入れたのかは、わたしは聞いたことがない。
さて巨人はたっぷり眠ったあと、腰掛けに横たわったまま体を伸ばしはじめて、こう呼ばわった。「じきにできるか。」
「いま始めたばかりです」と床几の上の一滴めの血が答えた。
そこで巨人はまた横になって眠り、長い長いあいだまどろんだ。とうとう少し寝返りを打ちはじめて、こう叫んだ。
「わしの言うことが聞こえるか。じきにできるか。」。だがこのときも最初と同じく顔を上げなかった。まだ半分眠っていたのである。
「半分できました」と二滴めの血が言った。
そこで巨人はまた名人娘だと思って、反対側へ寝返りを打ってまた眠り込んだ。そして何時間も眠りつづけたあと、身じろぎして老いた骨を伸ばしはじめ、こう呼ばわった。
「まだできんのか。」
「ちょうどよくできました」と三滴めの血が言った。
そこで巨人は起き上がって目をこすりはじめたが、自分に話しかけているのが誰か見えなかった。そこで名人娘を探して呼んだが、誰も答えなかった。

「まあよい! ちょっと外へ出たのだろう」と彼は思い、匙を取って鍋のところへスープを味わいに行った。ところが靴底とぼろとそんなものしか見つからず、それがみないっしょに煮えていて、どれが具でどれが汁かもわからなかった。それを見るやいなや事の次第を悟って、巨人はあまりの怒りにどちらの脚で立てばよいかもわからぬほどになった。そして風がうしろで鳴るほどの勢いで王子と名人娘を追って駆け出した。だがまもなく水に行き当たって渡れなくなった。
「かまうものか」と彼は言った。「これには手立てがある。わしの川飲みを呼べばよいのだ。」
そこで彼は川飲みを呼んだ。すると川飲みが来て身をかがめ、一口、二口、三口とがぶりと飲んだ。すると海の水がひどく減って、巨人には名人娘と王子が船で行くのが見えた。
「さあ、塩の塊を投げ捨てて」と名人娘は言った。
そこで王子がそれを舷から投げると、それは海を横切って高い山に育ち、巨人は越えられなくなった。そして川飲みももう水を飲み干して助けることができなくなった。
「かまうものか!」と巨人は叫んだ。「これにも手立てがある。」。そう言って山穿ちを呼んで山を穿たせ、川飲みが這い抜けてもう一度飲めるようにした。ところが山に穴を開けて川飲みが飲もうとしたちょうどそのとき、名人娘が王子に瓶から一、二滴投げ捨てるように言った。すると海はもとどおり満々となり、川飲みがもう一口飲む間もなく、二人は陸に着いて巨人から救われた。
そこで二人は王子の父のところへ帰ろうと決めたが、王子は名人娘を歩かせることなど聞こうともしなかった。娘にも自分にも似つかわしくないと思ったのである。
「ここで十分だけ待っていてくれ」と彼は言った。「父の厩にいる七頭の馬を取りに帰ってくる。大した道のりではないし、長くはかからない。いとしい人を歩かせて父の宮殿へ行かせるなど、聞く耳を持たないよ。」
「ああ!」と名人娘は言った。「どうかわたしを置いていかないで。いったん宮殿へ帰ったら、あなたはわたしをすっかり忘れてしまう。きっとそうなるわ。」
「なに!」と彼は言った。「どうしておまえを忘れられよう。これほど多くをともに切り抜けて、これほど深く愛しているおまえを。」
どうしようもなく、彼はどうしても馬車と七頭の馬を取りに帰ると言い、娘は海辺で待つことになった。そこでとうとう名人娘は彼の思うとおりにさせるほかなかった。ただこう言っただけだった。
「家に着いたら、誰にもこんにちはと言うために立ち止まりさえせず、まっすぐ厩へ行って馬をつなぎ、できるかぎり急いで戻ってきてください。みながあなたを取り囲むでしょうが、見えていないようにふるまうのです。そして何より、食べ物をひと口も口にしてはいけません。口にしたら、わたしたちは二人とも嘆きを見ることになります。」
王子はこれをみな約束した。だが心のなかではずっと、娘を忘れる恐れなどまずあるまいと思っていた。

さて彼が宮殿へ帰り着いたちょうどそのとき、兄の一人が婚礼の宴を開こうとしていて、花嫁とその縁者がみな宮殿に来たところだった。そこでみなが彼を取り囲んで、あれこれ尋ね、いっしょに中へ入ってくれと言った。だが彼は見えていないふりをして、まっすぐ厩へ行って馬を出し、つなぎはじめた。そして中へ入らせられそうにないと見ると、みなは食べ物と飲み物を、宴のために用意したいちばんよいものを持って外へ出てきた。だが王子はひと屑も口にせず、できるかぎり急いで馬をつないだ。とうとう花嫁の妹が林檎を一つ庭越しに転がしてよこして、こう言った。
「まあ、ほかに何も召し上がらないなら、せめてこれをひと口だけでも。こんなに長い旅のあとでは、お腹も空いて喉も渇いておいででしょうから。」
そこで彼は林檎を取り上げてひと口かじった。ところがそうするやいなや、名人娘のことも、娘を迎えに戻ることも忘れてしまった。
「わたしはどうかしているに違いない」と彼は言った。「この馬車と馬をどうしようというのだ。」。そう言って馬をまた厩に戻し、ほかの者たちといっしょに宮殿へ入っていった。そしてまもなく、林檎を転がしてよこした花嫁の妹と結婚することに決まった。

名人娘は海辺に坐って王子を待ちに待ったが、王子は来なかった。そこでとうとう岸から上がっていき、少し行ったところで、王の宮殿のすぐそばの雑木林にぽつんと建つ小さな小屋に着いた。娘は中へ入って、ここに泊めてもらえないかと尋ねた。小屋の主は老婆で、これまで見たこともないほどひねくれた口やかましい婆さんだった。はじめ婆さんは娘を泊めるなど聞こうともしなかったが、とうとう優しい言葉と高い宿賃のおかげで、名人娘はそこにいる許しを得た。さて小屋は豚小屋のように暗くて汚かったので、名人娘は、家のなかがほかの人の家のように見えるように少し小ぎれいにしましょうと言った。老婆はこれも気に入らず、歯をむき出して不機嫌だった。だが名人娘は気にも留めなかった。娘は黄金の櫃を取って、ひとつかみほどを火に投げ込んだ。すると見よ! 黄金は溶けて、泡立って炉からあふれ出し、小屋じゅうに広がって、外も内も金めっきしてしまった。ところが黄金が泡立って煮えはじめるやいなや、老婆は怖くなって、悪魔にかかとを追われているかのように駆け出そうとした。そして戸から駆け出すとき身をかがめるのを忘れて、鴨居に頭をしたたか打ちつけ、首の骨を折って、それで死んでしまった。
翌朝、代官がその道を通りかかった。そして雑木林のなかで黄金の小屋が輝ききらめいているのを見て、自分の目が信じられぬほどだったことはお察しのとおりである。だが中に入って、そこに坐っている美しい乙女を見たときには、いっそう驚いた。手短に言えば、代官は乙女に首ったけになって、どうか妻になってくれと頼み込んだ。
「まあ、それでお金はたくさんお持ちですか」と名人娘は尋ねた。
ええ、それについては、そう悪い暮らし向きではありませんよ、と代官は言って、金を取りに家へ帰った。そして夕方に戻ってくると、半ブッシェルの袋を持ってきて腰掛けの上に置いた。そこで名人娘は、これほど金持ちなら連れ合いになりましょうと言った。ところが床につくかつかないかのうちに、娘はまた起きねばならないと言った。
「火を熾しておくのを忘れてしまいましたから。」
「どうか寝床から動かないで」と代官は言った。「わたしがやりましょう。」
そう言って寝床から跳び起き、たちまち炉端に立った。
「十能をつかんだら、すぐに教えてくださいね」と名人娘は言った。
「いま持っているよ」と代官は言った。
すると名人娘はこう言った。
「神の御心により、あなたが十能を持ち、十能があなたを持ち、朝が来るまであなたが自分の上に熱い燃える炭をかけつづけますように。」

そうして代官は一晩じゅうそこに立って、自分の上に熱い燃える炭をかけつづけた。そしてどれほど頼み、祈り、泣いても、炭は少しも冷たくならなかった。だが夜が明けて十能を投げ捨てる力が戻るやいなや、彼は長居せず——お察しのとおり——悪魔か執達吏にかかとを追われているかのように駆け去った。そして出会う者はみな目玉が飛び出るほど彼を見つめた。彼が気でも狂ったように跳ね回っていたからである。そして皮を剝がれてなめされたとしても、これよりひどい姿にはなれなかったろう。そして誰もが彼に何があったのかと不思議がったが、彼は恥ずかしさのあまり、どこにいたのか誰にも話さなかった。
翌日、代訴人が名人娘の住むところを通りかかった。そして彼もまた、雑木林のなかで小屋が輝ききらめいているのを見た。そこで誰が小屋の持ち主かを知ろうと脇へ逸れた。そして中に入って美しい乙女を見ると、代官よりもいっそう恋に落ちて、大慌てで口説きはじめた。

さて名人娘は、代官に尋ねたのと同じように、お金はたっぷりお持ちですかと尋ねた。すると代訴人は、そう悪い暮らし向きではないと言い、その証しに金を取りに家へ帰った。そして夕方に、大きく膨れた金の袋を持って戻ってきた——まるまる一ブッシェルの袋だったと思う——そして腰掛けの上に置いた。そして事のあらましを言えば、彼は娘を得ることになり、二人は床についた。ところが名人娘は突然、玄関の戸を閉め忘れていた、起きて夜のあいだ閉めておかねばならないと言った。
「なに、あなたがそれをするですって!」と代訴人は言った。「わたしがここに寝ているのに。とんでもない。じっとしていてください。わたしが行ってやりましょう。」
そう言って太鼓の上の豆のように跳び起き、玄関へ駆け出した。
「戸の掛け金をつかんだら教えてくださいね」と名人娘は言った。
「いま持っているよ」と代訴人は言った。
「では神の御心により」と名人娘は言った。「あなたが戸を持ち、戸があなたを持ち、夜が明けるまであなたが壁から壁へと行きますように。」

そこで代訴人が一晩じゅうどんな踊りを踊ったか、お察しのとおりである。あんなワルツは踊ったことがなかったし、二度と踊らずに済むならそれに越したことはないと思ったことだろう。戸を手前に引けば戸が彼を引き戻し、そうして彼は玄関の一方の隅へ叩きつけられ、次にもう一方の隅へと、あやうく打ち殺されるほどになった。はじめは呪って罵り、それから頼んで祈ったが、戸は夜明けまで自分の側を守り通すことしか気にかけなかった。そして戸が手を放すやいなや、代訴人は一夜の宿賃として金を置いたまま駆け去り、求婚のこともすっかり忘れてしまった。というのも正直なところ、家の戸が踊りながら追いかけてくるのではないかと恐れていたのである。出会う者はみな彼を見つめて口をあんぐり開けた。彼もまた狂人のように跳ね回っていたからである。そして牡羊の群れに一晩じゅう頭突きをして過ごしたとしても、これよりひどい姿にはなれなかったろう。

三日めには郡代がその道を通りかかった。そして彼もまた黄金の小屋を見て、そこに誰が住んでいるのかを知ろうと脇へ逸れた。そして名人娘に目を留めるやいなや口説きはじめた。そこで娘はほかの二人に答えたのと同じように答えた。金をたっぷり持っているなら連れ合いになろう、そうでなければ自分の用に行くがよい、と。さて郡代は、そう悪い暮らし向きではない、家へ帰って金を取ってこようと言った。そして夕方にまた来ると、代訴人のよりさらに大きな袋を持っていた——少なくとも一ブッシェル半はあったに違いない——そしてそれを腰掛けの上に置いた。そこでまもなく、彼が名人娘を得ることに決まった。ところが床につくかつかないかのうちに、名人娘は、牧場から仔牛を連れ帰るのを忘れていた、起きて厩へ追い込まねばならないと言った。すると郡代は、あらゆる力にかけてそんなことはさせぬと誓い、太って頑丈な体で、仔猫のようにすばやく跳び起きた。
「では、仔牛の尻尾をつかんだら教えてくださいね」と名人娘は言った。
「いま持っているぞ」と郡代は言った。
「神の御心により」と名人娘は言った。「あなたが仔牛の尻尾を持ち、仔牛の尻尾があなたを持ち、夜が明けるまで二人で世界をひとめぐりしますように。」

さて、郡代がどれほど脚を伸ばさねばならなかったか、お察しのとおりである。仔牛と彼は高きも低きも越え、丘も谷も越えて駆けていった。そして郡代が呪い罵れば罵るほど、仔牛は速く走り跳ねた。夜明けには哀れな郡代は息も絶え絶えで、仔牛の尻尾を放せるのがあまりに嬉しくて、金の袋もそのほか何もかも忘れてしまった。彼は偉い人だったので代訴人や代官より少しゆっくり歩いたが、ゆっくり歩けば歩くほど、人々には彼を眺めて見つめる時間が増えた。そして人々がその時間を存分に使ったことは言うまでもあるまい。仔牛との踊りのあとで、彼はひどく裂けてぼろぼろになっていたからである。

翌日は宮殿での婚礼の日と定められていて、いちばん上の兄が花嫁と馬車で教会へ行き、巨人のもとで暮らしていた弟が花嫁の妹と行くことになっていた。ところが馬車に乗り込んで出発しようというとき、引き綱の留め栓が一本折れた。そして少なくとも三本は代わりを作ったが、どんな材の木で作ってもみな折れてしまった。そうして時が過ぎに過ぎて教会へ行けず、誰もがひどく気落ちした。ところが突然、代官が——彼も婚礼に招かれていたのである——あちらの雑木林に乙女が一人住んでいると言った。
「その娘から、火を熾すのに使う十能の柄を借りることさえできれば、それはきっともつでしょう。」
さて! みなはその場で使いを出し、たいそう丁重な口上を乙女に伝えて、代官の言った十能を貸してもらえないかと尋ねさせた。すると乙女は「はい」と言い、貸してくれた。こうして折れそうにない引き綱の留め栓が手に入った。

ところが突然、まさに出発しようというときに、馬車の底が粉々に崩れてしまった。そこでみなは精一杯新しい底を作りにかかった。だが何本釘を打とうと、どんな材の木で作ろうと同じことで、底をうまく馬車に嵌めて出発しようとするやいなや、ぱきりと二つに割れてしまい、引き綱の留め栓をなくしたときよりさらに困り果てた。ちょうどそのとき代訴人が言った——代官がそこにいたのだから、代訴人もいたのはお察しのとおりである——「あちらの雑木林に乙女が一人住んでいて、その娘から玄関の戸の半分を借りることさえできれば、それはきっともちましょう。」

さて! みなはまた雑木林へ使いを出し、代訴人の言った金めっきの玄関の戸を貸してもらえないかとたいそう丁重に尋ねさせた。するとその場で貸してもらえた。そこでいよいよ出発しようとした。ところが今度は馬の力が足りず、六頭いても馬車を引けなかった。そこで八頭にし、十頭にし、十二頭にしたが、増やせば増やすほど、そして御者が鞭を打てば打つほど、馬車は一寸も動かなかった。このころにはもう日がだいぶ高くなっていて、宮殿の誰もが嘆きに沈んでいた。教会へは行かねばならぬのに、どうやっても着けそうになかったのである。そこでとうとう郡代が、あちらの雑木林の金めっきの小屋に乙女が一人住んでいて、その仔牛を借りることさえできれば、と言った。
「あれなら、山ほど重かろうと馬車を引けましょう。」

さて、仔牛に教会まで引かせるなど間抜けに見えようとみな思ったが、どうしようもなかった。そこで三度めの使いを出し、王の名においてたいそう丁重に、郡代の言った仔牛を借りられないかと尋ねさせた。すると名人娘はその場で貸してくれた。今度も「いいえ」と言う気はなかったのである。そこで仔牛を馬の前につないで、役に立つかどうか見ていると、馬車は高きも低きも、切り株も石も越えて駆け出し、みな息もつけぬほどだった。あるときは地上にいて、あるときは空の上にいた。そして教会に着くと、仔牛はその周りを糸紡ぎ機のようにぐるぐる走りはじめたので、みなは馬車から降りて教会に入るのに難儀した。帰りも同じことで、ただ行きより速かった。そして出発したと思う間もなく宮殿に着いていた。
さて一同が食卓についたとき、巨人に仕えていた王子が、十能の柄と玄関の戸と仔牛を貸してくれた乙女を宮殿へ招くべきだと思うと言った。
「というのも」と彼は言った。「この三つがなかったら、われらはいまでもここで立ち往生していたでしょうから。」
そうだ、王もそれがまったく道理だと思い、いちばんよい家来五人を金めっきの小屋へ遣わして、王から乙女に挨拶を伝え、宮殿へ来て食事をともにしてくださらぬかと尋ねさせた。
「王さまにご挨拶を」と名人娘は言った。「そしてこうお伝えください。あの方がわたしのところへ来られぬほど高貴でいらっしゃるなら、わたしもあの方のところへ行けぬほど高貴です、と。」
そこで王は自分で出向かねばならなくなった。すると名人娘は何も言わずに王とともに上がっていった。そして王は、この娘は見かけ以上の者だと思ったので、いちばん下の花婿のかたわらの最上席に坐らせた。
さて食卓に少し坐っていると、名人娘は巨人のところから持ち出した黄金の林檎と、黄金の雄鶏と雌鶏を取り出して、自分の前の卓に置いた。すると雄鶏と雌鶏はたちまちつつき合い、黄金の林檎を争いはじめた。
「おお! ごらんなさい」と王子は言った。「あの二羽が林檎を取り合っている。」
「ええ!」と名人娘は言った。「あのころ、丘のなかでいっしょにいたときに逃げ出そうとしたわたしたち二人も、ああでした。」
するとそのとき呪縛が解けて、王子は彼女が誰かを思い出した。そしてどれほど喜んだかはお察しのとおりである。だが彼に林檎を転がしてよこしたあの魔女については、二十四頭の馬に引き裂かせて一片も残らぬようにした。そしてそのあと、婚礼が本気ではじまった。そして代官も代訴人も郡代も、体はまだこわばって足は痛んでいたが、誰にも負けぬほど賑わいを続けた。
